I pick **Candidate 3**, with moderate confidence. I worked this out roughly from the forecast averages; nothing was simulated. Candidates 3 and 5 could come out close.

**How the order schedules compare:**
- **Fixed ordering cost.** Candidate 7 orders every day, about 27 orders, so it pays about 567 in fixed costs. That is roughly 380 more than the every-3-days plans (9 orders). Ordering every day does cut holding and spoilage, but not by enough to cover 380. Candidate 5 orders every 2 days (14 orders, about 294), about 105 more than the 3-day plans. It does hold less of product 0, so the two may be close. Even so, the 3-day schedule looks a little better.
- **Product 1 shelf life.** Product 1 keeps 4 days. In the 4-day plans (1, 4, 6), each batch spoils the evening before the next one arrives. Nothing is left over to cover the next cycle, so anything above demand is thrown away. In the 3-day plans the batches overlap by one day: oldest stock sells first, so up to about one day's demand of leftover still gets sold. That makes extra stock cheap. The 4-day plans also run close to the 192-unit capacity (about 130 of product 1 plus about 60–80 of product 0). Candidate 1 is the worst here: its 78–96 units of product 0 make overflow likely.

**Choosing among 0, 2 and 3.** These three use the same schedule and differ only in size. Compared with the forecast for the days each order covers, Candidate 0 orders about 1.0×, Candidate 2 about 1.1×, and Candidate 3 about 1.2× for product 0 and about 1.1× for product 1.
- **Product 0:** a missed unit costs 11 (3 lost margin plus the 8 penalty). Leftovers keep 8 days and cost only 0.7 a day to hold. Ordering above the forecast pays off.
- **Product 1:** a missed unit costs 5. Leftovers are partly sold because the batches overlap, so a margin above the forecast also helps.
- Actual demand runs about 4.6% above the forecast on average, which is one more reason to order above it.

**Risks for Candidate 3:**
- Around days 18–19 (the 83 units of product 0 arrive on day 18, then the 126 units of product 1 on day 19), the warehouse will overflow by about 10 units. Candidate 2 would lose about 4. That costs only tens.
- Cash is tight after the day 3 order (about 300 left), but it is enough to pay for the next order in full.

I pick **candidate 5**. It is close to candidate 7, and I didn't do a full day-by-day simulation of every plan. I estimated each plan's costs roughly, in my head.

**Same for every plan.** No order arrives before day 3 for item 0 or before day 4 for item 1, so the shortages at the start are the same for all candidates. Item 0 runs short by about 9 units over days 0–2. Item 1 runs short by about 70 units over days 0–3.

**The main trade-off is order fees against holding cost.** Both items earn 3 per unit sold, so how often a plan orders matters most.

- **Every 4 days (candidates 1, 4, 6): ruled out.**
  - Candidates 1 and 6 order 203 units in one go, more than the 192 the warehouse holds. Candidate 4 orders 188, so with stock left over, units are lost when deliveries arrive.
  - Each batch of item 1 has to cover exactly 4 days of shelf life, with no slack.
  - Holding costs about 105 per cycle in extra stock, but ordering less often saves only about 63 in fees.
- **Every 3 days (candidates 0, 2, 3): weaker.**
  - Each cycle saves 42 in fees but adds about 52 in holding (item 0 costs 0.7 per unit per day to store).
  - Candidate 0 orders item 1 below forecast (100 against 109), so it loses sales.
  - Candidate 3 orders 12–24% above forecast and nearly fills the warehouse around day 19.
  - Candidate 2 is the best of this group, but it is still behind the next two.
- **Daily (candidate 7) or every 2 days (candidate 5): the leaders.**
  - Ordering daily costs 27 × 21 = 567 in fees. Ordering every 2 days costs about 294, which saves about 273.
  - Candidate 5 pays extra holding of roughly 17–18 per cycle, about 246 over the month. On these numbers the two are almost tied.

**Randomness tips it to candidate 5.** Each of its orders covers two days of demand, so random ups and downs partly cancel out. Its orders sit about 20% above forecast for item 0 and about 5% above for item 1. That fits the costs: running out of item 0 loses 11 per unit (the 8 penalty plus the lost 3 margin), and on average demand runs about 4.6% above forecast. Both its last deliveries also land by days 28–29, so nothing is paid for and lost after day 29.

I chose **candidate 2**. I worked the plans through by hand on the forecast values, roughly, with no simulation run, and the gap between candidates 2, 0 and 7 is small.

1. **Candidate 7 (orders every day)** pays the 21 ordering fee 27 times, about 567. Each order equals the forecast, so with random demand it will often run short. A missing unit of good 0 costs 11 (penalty 8 plus the lost margin of 3). Its lower storage cost does not make up for the extra fees.
2. **Candidate 5 (orders every 2 days)** carries very little safety stock, about 5%, so it also runs short. It pays about 294 in ordering fees.
3. **Candidates 1, 4 and 6 (orders every 4 days):**
   - Shelf life of good 1 is 4 days, exactly one cycle, so any good 1 left at the end of a cycle is written off.
   - The warehouse limit of 192 is nearly reached even on forecast values: on day 4, candidate 1 has 69 + 123 = 192 and candidate 6 has 59 + 133 = 192.
   - Candidate 1's day-12 order of 134 units of good 1 has to cover forecast demand of 167 over days 16–19, so it falls short.
4. **Candidates 0, 2 and 3 (orders every 3 days)** pay about 189 in ordering fees, and good 1 sells out within its shelf life. They differ only in safety stock:
   - **Candidate 0** orders exactly the forecast, so it runs short whenever demand comes in above forecast.
   - **Candidate 3** (about +20%) overflows the warehouse on day 19 even on forecast values. It would hold about 76 + 11 + 126 = 213, so about 21 units of good 1 are lost. With random demand it would also have more good 1 written off.
   - **Candidate 2** (about +10%) is the best fit. It has a buffer against shortages, which cost more than the storage. It overflows by only about 4 units on day 19.

I pick **Candidate 7**. Every estimate here was done roughly in my head, and Candidate 7 and Candidate 5 come out very close.

**1. Orders every 3–4 days (Candidates 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6).** These save on the 21-per-order fee: about 7–9 orders, or roughly 150–190. They lose more than that on storage, though. A batch meant for several days stays in the warehouse about 1–1.5 nights per unit on average:
- product 0: about 0.7 × ~500 units ≈ 350 or more;
- product 1: about 0.2 × ~960 units ≈ 190 or more.

Taken together, that is clearly more than the order-fee savings. The larger plans also risk hitting the 192 limit. In Candidate 3, around day 19 about 70 units of product 0 are still in stock when 126 units of product 1 arrive. That makes about 196, so the extra is lost. On top of that, ordering every 4 days for product 1 (shelf life 4 days) leaves no slack. If demand turns out low, the leftover gets written off.

**2. Daily orders (Candidate 7).** The order fees are about 27 × 21 = 567, but there is almost no batch stock sitting in storage. Quantities track the forecast for day t + L:
- product 0: about 1.15–1.2 × forecast. That makes sense, because running short costs 8 per unit, more than the margin of 3.
- product 1: about 1.03 × forecast, which is roughly the average demand.

Leftovers carry over to the next day and soften the randomness. The warehouse limit and starting cash are not a problem.

**3. Orders every 2 days (Candidate 5).** Order fees are about 294, and storage adds roughly 270 more. The total is close to Candidate 7. However, its product 1 quantities sit right at the average demand while covering two days at once. That means somewhat more shortages and penalties when demand jumps.

Candidate 7 should have the highest expected profit, with Candidate 5 just behind it.

**Выбор: кандидат 2.** Уверенность умеренная: кандидаты 5 и 7 отстают ненамного, порядка сотни. Всё ниже посчитано в уме, грубо, на прогнозных значениях; симуляцию по дням я не запускал.

**Что общее у всех планов**
- Первые дни все кандидаты проходят одинаково. Стартовых 50 ед. товара 1 не хватает на дни 0–3 (прогноз около 120), и до дня 4 заказ не придёт ни у кого. Товара 0 до дня 3 тоже немного не хватает.
- Средний множитель спроса около 1,046. Значит, заказ ровно по прогнозу в среднем чуть меньше фактического спроса.

**Как устроены кандидаты**
- **0, 2, 3** заказывают раз в 3 дня, всего 9 заказов, 189 за заказы. Это один план с разным запасом. Товара 0 они берут примерно 1,0×, 1,1× и 1,25× прогноза. Товара 1 — примерно 0,94×, 1,04× и 1,12×.
- **1, 4, 6** заказывают раз в 4 дня. Товар 1 годен 4 дня, поэтому каждая партия должна разойтись ровно за свой цикл: остаток нельзя продать позже, он сразу списывается. Кроме того, партии около 80 ед. товара 0 плюс около 125 ед. товара 1 близки к вместимости 192 или превышают её, и излишек пропадает.
- **5** заказывает раз в 2 дня (13 заказов, 273). Товар 0 берёт около 1,2× прогноза.
- **7** заказывает каждый день (27 заказов, 567). Товар 0 берёт около 1,15× прогноза.

**Почему кандидат 2**
- **Товар 0.** План не пересчитывается по факту, поэтому излишек товара 0 каждый цикл копится. Срок годности 8 дней, а старые партии продаются первыми, так что списание этот запас почти не срезает. Хранение стоит 0,7 за единицу в день.
  - У кандидатов 5 и 7 к концу набирается 40–50 лишних единиц, это примерно 400–500 на хранении.
  - У кандидата 2 — около 20 единиц, примерно 190.
  - У кандидата 0 запаса нет, и он теряет на нехватке: 8 неустойки плюс 3 упущенной маржи за каждую единицу.
- **Итог по затратам (оценка).** Заказы, хранение, списания и нехватка дают примерно 875 у кандидата 2, около 970 у кандидата 7 и около 1070 у кандидата 5.
- **Товар 1.** У кандидата 2 заказ почти совпадает с ожидаемым спросом. Это разумно: остаток товара 1 продаётся ещё один день, а нехватка стоит недорого (2 неустойки).
- **Кандидат 3** запасает больше всех. Около дня 19 (крупный приход товара 0, затем 126 ед. товара 1) склад переполняется: теряется примерно 20–27 ед. товара 1. У кандидата 2 в тот же момент переполнение около 9 ед., у кандидата 0 его нет.
- **Устойчивость.** Если спрос отклонится от прогноза, вариант с умеренным запасом (кандидат 2) пострадает меньше, чем вариант без запаса (кандидат 0) или с избыточным (кандидат 3).

I picked **candidate 5**. I worked it out by hand from the rules, without running a simulation, so this is a judgement call. The margin over candidate 2 is small.

**The trade-off.** Ordering more often costs more in fixed fees (21 per order day) but cuts holding cost and spoilage.

| Order cycle | Candidates | Order days | Fixed cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Daily | 7 | 27 | 567 |
| Every 2 days | 5 | 14 | 294 |
| Every 3 days | 0, 2, 3 | 9 | 189 |
| Every 4 days | 1, 4, 6 | 7 | 147 |

**Why not the others:**
- **4-day plans (1, 4, 6):** they save only about 42 in fees over the 3-day plans. In return, product 0 sits in stock longer at 0.7 per unit per day, and product 1 has to cover all 4 days of its shelf life with no buffer. Candidate 6 also goes over the 192-unit warehouse limit around day 4, and the excess is lost.
- **Daily plan (7):** it pays about 378 more in fees than the 3-day plans. It saves only about 270 in holding cost, so it comes out behind.
- **3-day plans (0, 2, 3):** these differ in how much stock they hold beyond the forecast. Candidate 0 orders roughly the forecast, candidate 2 about 12% more, candidate 3 about 24% more. For product 0 a shortage costs about 11 per unit, while a leftover unit costs only about 2 because it keeps for 8 days and sells in the next cycle. So buffer stock pays off. For product 1 a shortage costs about 5 and an expired unit about 7.5, so you should order close to the forecast. Candidate 2 is the best balance of the three.

**Candidate 5 vs candidate 2.** Candidate 5 pays about 105 more in fees. It gets back roughly 235 in lower holding cost: about 135 on product 0 and about 100 on product 1. Product 1 lasts 4 days and candidate 5 orders every 2 days, so leftovers from one delivery still sell during the next cycle. That means less spoilage when actual demand differs from the forecast. Its order sizes are about 5–20% above the forecast, which matches the costs above.

I pick **candidate 5**, which orders every 2 days. I worked this out by hand, not with a full simulation, so the call between 5 and 7 is only moderately confident.

**Losses common to every plan.** No order can arrive before day 3 for product 0 or day 4 for product 1. The starting 22 units of product 0 run about 9 short over days 0–2. The starting 50 units of product 1 run about 70 short over days 0–3. These penalties are the same for all candidates, so they don't change the ranking.

**Main trade-off: fixed order fees against holding cost.**
- Holding product 0 costs 0.7 per unit per day, which is large next to its margin of 3. Each extra day of cover adds roughly 0.5 day of demand to average stock. That is about 9 per day across both products, or around 240 over the horizon.
- Each extra ordering day costs 21.
- **Candidate 7 (orders daily):** 27 order days cost 567. That is 273 more than ordering every 2 days, and it saves only about 240 in holding.
- **Candidates 0, 2, 3 (every 3 days):** they save about 105 in fees compared with every 2 days, but pay about 240 more in holding.
- **Candidates 1, 4, 6 (every 4 days):** holding is higher still. They also nearly fill the 192-unit warehouse: about 133 units of product 1 arrive while about 55–70 units of product 0 are still in stock. Candidate 1, which orders up to 96 of product 0, will overflow and lose stock.

**Order sizes in candidate 5 against the forecast:**
- **Product 0:** it orders about 1.2 times forecast demand. That suits this product, because a shortage costs 11 (penalty 8 plus the lost margin of 3), while extra stock just carries over at 0.7 per day.
- **Product 1:** it orders about 1.05 times forecast, which roughly matches the average demand multiplier of 1.046. With 2 days of cover and a 4-day shelf life, little goes to waste.
- **Capacity:** it stays under 192, including the large order of 122 on day 14, which arrives for the demand peak on days 18–19.

**Robustness.** Candidate 7 orders thinner on product 0 (about 1.15 times forecast) and almost exactly at forecast on product 1 (about 1.02). That makes it more exposed to the expensive shortages when actual demand runs higher than the forecast.

I'd go with **candidate 5**. I estimated this in my head, without simulating any of the plans, so it's a judgement call. Candidates 5 and 7 come out close.

**Ruled out first: candidates 1, 4, 6 (one order every 4 days).** Each order is very large, often 180–230 units for the two goods together. With leftover stock already on the shelves, part of each delivery won't fit the 192-unit store and is lost after being paid for. Good 1 also only lasts 4 days, so it has no buffer for the gap until the next delivery.

**The rest is a trade-off between ordering costs and storage costs.** If each order covers n days, the stock left on the shelf each evening averages about (n−1)/2 days of demand. One day of stock costs about 16 × 0.7 + 32 × 0.2 ≈ 17.6 a day in storage.

| Plan | Orders | Fee of 21 per order | Extra storage over the period | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Every day (7) | 27 | ≈ 567 | ≈ 0 | ≈ 567 |
| Every 2 days (5) | 13 | ≈ 273 | ≈ 240 | ≈ 513 |
| Every 3 days (0, 2, 3) | 9 | ≈ 189 | ≈ 480 | ≈ 669 |

**Why 5 within the every-2-days approach:**
- **Order sizes look right.** Good 0 is ordered at about 1.2 × forecast. That margin makes sense because running out of good 0 costs 8 per unit, much more than the 0.7 storage. Good 1 is ordered close to forecast (about 1.05×), because its shortage cost is only 2.
- **Capacity is safe.** Two days of stock fits in 192 units with room to spare.
- **Demand is smoother.** Covering two days per order evens out the daily random swings a little, so there are fewer shortages than with daily ordering.

Among the every-3-days plans, candidate 0 under-orders good 1 (about 0.92 × forecast). Candidate 3 over-orders, and its day-15 order alone is 209 units, more than the store holds. Candidate 2 is reasonable, but the extra storage costs should still put it behind 5.

I picked candidate 2. I estimated this in my head without running a simulation, so the 2-versus-3 call is a judgement, not a calculated result.

**Fixed ordering cost (21 per day with any order):**
- Candidate 7 orders almost every day: 27 × 21 = 567.
- Candidate 5 orders every 2 days: 14 × 21 = 294.
- Candidates 0, 2 and 3 order every 3 days: 9 × 21 = 189.
- Candidates 1, 4 and 6 order every 4 days: 7 × 21 = 147.

**Weak options:**
- **4-day cycle (1, 4, 6).** Each order of product 1 is 112–145 units, on top of 60–96 units of product 0. Together that is near or over the 192-unit warehouse limit, so stock is regularly lost on arrival. The lost units are already paid for at 4 and 7 each.
- **Candidate 7.** It matches demand closely, but costs about 380 more in ordering fees than a 3-day cycle. Shelf stock carries over between orders in both schemes, so ordering daily doesn't buy enough accuracy to make that up.
- **Candidate 5.** It also pays more in fees and still misses demand in places.

**Choosing among the 3-day plans (0, 2, 3).** I compared each plan's order size with the forecast demand for the days that delivery covers. Actual demand averages about 1.046 × forecast, so a plan at 1.0 is short on average.
- **Product 0:** a shortage costs 11 (lost margin 3 plus penalty 8). Excess costs only 0.7 per day in storage and keeps for 8 days, so stocking about 1.2 × forecast is worth it.
  - Candidate 0 orders about 1.0 × forecast, so it runs short.
  - Candidate 2 orders about 1.11 ×.
  - Candidate 3 orders about 1.24 ×.
- **Product 1:** a shortage costs 5, while an unsold unit can expire and lose 7. The best level is roughly 1.0–1.05 × forecast, allowing for some carry-over.
  - Candidate 0 orders about 0.92 ×, which is too little.
  - Candidate 2 orders about 1.03 ×, which is about right.
  - Candidate 3 orders about 1.12 ×, which means more expired stock.
- **Capacity:** candidate 3 is more likely to lose stock to the warehouse limit, especially when the large orders arrive on days 18–19.

Candidate 2 is the best balance: product 0 slightly over-stocked, product 1 close to the target, and less risk of losing stock to the space limit.

**Recommendation: candidate 5.** The margin over candidate 7 is small, under about 40 per 30 days. That's inside the error of my rough estimate, so this is a lean, not a confident pick. I worked it out by hand from expected values and didn't simulate it.

**What's the same for every plan**
- The first product 1 delivery can't arrive before day 4. The opening 50 units cover days 0–3, where expected demand is 120, so everyone loses the same amount there.
- Product 0 runs short on day 2 in every plan, for the same reason.
- Both products earn 3 per unit sold. The real differences are order costs (21 per order day), holding costs (high for product 0 at 0.7 per day), unsold product 1 expiring, and running out.

**Plans that order every 4 days (1, 4, 6)**
- These are the weakest group.
- A product 1 delivery has to last all 4 days of its shelf life. It can't share stock with the next delivery, so leftovers expire.
- Product 0 sits in stock longer. That adds roughly 150 in holding costs while saving only 42 in order fees.
- The warehouse runs near its 192-unit limit. Candidate 1 is close to overflowing when its deliveries arrive, and anything over the limit is lost.

**Plans that order every 3 days (0, 2, 3)**
- These differ only in size, against expected demand of about 1.05 × forecast:
  - Candidate 0 orders about 0.92 of the forecast for product 1 and runs short too often.
  - Candidate 2 orders about 1.03 for product 1, which is close to ideal.
  - Candidate 3 orders about 1.24 for product 0, which suits that product, but it also nears the warehouse limit around days 18–19.
- Compared with ordering every 2 days, they hold more stock on average. That costs about 150 more for product 0 and about 85 more for product 1, against only about 105 saved in order fees.

**Candidate 5 (every 2 days)**
- Order fees are 14 × 21 = 294.
- Sizing looks right: about 1.2 × forecast for product 0, where running out costs 11 per unit and storing costs little, and about 1.05 for product 1.
- Each product 1 delivery overlaps the next one by 2 days. Leftovers are sold first, so less expires and random swings in demand are absorbed better.
- It never comes near the warehouse limit.

**Candidate 7 (daily)**
- Its sizing is similar to candidate 5: about 1.15 for product 0 and 1.02 for product 1.
- Daily ordering costs about 273 more in order fees (27 × 21 = 567). The extra holding it saves is only about 237 (around 151 for product 0 and 86 for product 1). On my numbers that's a near tie.

Я выбрал кандидата 2 по прикидке в уме, ничего не моделировал, так что это оценка, а не точный расчёт.

1. **Частота заказов.** Каждый заказ стоит 21, поэтому ежедневные заказы (кандидат 7) обходятся примерно в 567. Это больше, чем они экономят на хранении. План с заказом раз в два дня (кандидат 5) по моей прикидке примерно равен планам с заказом раз в три дня: экономия на хранении товара 0 около 113 против лишних 105 на заказах. Но у трёхдневных планов есть небольшое преимущество: случайные колебания спроса сглаживаются на трёх днях, а не на двух.
2. **Заказ раз в четыре дня (кандидаты 1, 4, 6).** Товар 1 годен 4 дня, поэтому каждая партия должна закрыть ровно свои 4 дня, и остаток в следующий цикл не переходит. Кроме того, товар 0 дольше лежит на складе за 0,7 в день, а крупные приходы скорее упрутся во вместимость 192.
3. **Объём заказа среди трёхдневных планов (кандидаты 0, 2, 3).** Это один план в разных масштабах. Кандидат 0 заказывает примерно по прогнозу или меньше: товар 1 около 0,92–1,0 от прогноза на три дня. С учётом того, что средний множитель 1,046, он будет часто не покрывать спрос. У кандидата 3 товар 1 около 1,12 от прогноза. Это слишком много, потому что остаток товара 1 почти весь списывается. Кандидат 2 даёт по товару 1 около 1,03, а по товару 0 около 1,11.
4. **Почему такие запасы правильные.** Для товара 0 нехватка дорогая: 3 упущенной маржи плюс 8 неустойки. Излишек дешёвый, потому что товар годен 8 дней и переходит в следующий цикл. Поэтому запас сверху оправдан. Для товара 1 нехватка стоит около 5, а излишек около 7, так как остаток в основном пропадает. Поэтому заказ должен быть близок к ожидаемому спросу. Кандидат 2 подходит под оба условия лучше остальных.

I'd pick **candidate 2**. I did this by rough mental estimates, not a full day-by-day calculation, and the lead over 3, 5 and 7 is fairly small.

1. **Start of the period is the same for everyone.** No order arrives before day 3 for item 0 or day 4 for item 1. Every plan runs short at the start, about 9 units of item 0 and about 70 of item 1, so this doesn't separate them.

2. **Ordering every 4 days (candidates 1, 4, 6) runs into warehouse space.** One batch has to cover 4 days: about 70–95 units of item 0 plus 110–145 of item 1. That hits the 192-unit limit. In candidate 1, by day 4 about 70 units of item 0 are still in stock when 123 units of item 1 arrive, so some of the delivery is lost. Candidate 6 is worse still. Item 1 also keeps only 4 days, so it has no slack: any leftover gets written off. Candidate 4 roughly fits the space but carries the same spoilage risk.

3. **More frequent ordering (candidates 5 and 7) costs more in fixed fees.** The fee is 21 for each day with an order. That comes to about 567 for candidate 7 (27 order days) and 273 for candidate 5, versus 189 for the every-3-days plans. The plan is fixed in advance, so ordering daily doesn't let you react to actual demand. It also pools leftovers less well. The extra fees aren't paid back.

4. **Choosing among the every-3-days plans (0, 2, 3).** The space limit isn't a problem for any of them. What differs is the safety margin over forecast demand:
   - **Candidate 0** orders about exactly the forecast. Average demand is about 4.6% above the forecast, so it falls short slightly but systematically. A shortage costs 11 per unit of item 0 (3 lost margin + 8 penalty) and 5 per unit of item 1 (3 + 2).
   - **Candidate 2** orders about 1.1× the forecast. For item 0 that is a sensible buffer: shortages are expensive, unsold stock lasts 8 days, and storage is only 0.7 a day. For item 1 the excess is moderate, and leftovers can still be sold on the next batch's first day before they expire.
   - **Candidate 3** orders about 1.2× the forecast. For item 1 that means more write-offs: each spoiled unit loses its purchase price of 7.

Candidate 2 has the best expected profit and is also steady when actual demand moves away from the forecast.

- В планах 1, 4, 6 (раз в 4 дня) остаток партии списывается вечером накануне прихода следующей, так что весь излишек пропадает. Кроме того, партии большие, и склад на 192 единицы почти полон в дни 8, 12, 16 и 24. В дни 12, 16 и 24 запас оказывается на 191–194 единицах, то есть при случайном росте запаса часть прихода теряется. Экономия на трёх-четырёх фиксированных платежах (примерно 42–63) этого не окупает.

**Объёмы в планах с циклом 3 дня.** Средний спрос равен прогнозу × ~1,046.
- **План 0** заказывает меньше среднего спроса. По товару 1 не хватает примерно 14 единиц за цикл. Каждая такая единица стоит 5 (упущенная маржа 3 плюс неустойка 2), то есть всего около 600 потерь. Товара 0 тоже в среднем немного не хватает, а неустойка за него высокая (11 за единицу).
- **План 3** заказывает товар 0 с запасом около 25% к среднему спросу. Излишек копится примерно на 9–14 единиц за цикл, а годность 8 дней этот излишек не сжигает. К дню 19 запас товара 0 доходит примерно до 110 единиц. В тот же день приходит 126 единиц товара 1, и склад переполняется. Добавляется хранение 0,7 за единицу в день на десятки лишних единиц.
- **План 2** заказывает примерно по среднему спросу: товар 1 почти точно, товар 0 с излишком около 3–4 единиц за цикл. Склад он почти не переполняет: в день 19 выходит около 196 единиц, то есть теряется всего около 4.
- **Планы 5 и 7** заказывают раз в 2 дня и каждый день, это даёт 273 и 567 фиксированных платежей против 189. Плану нужно составить заранее, поэтому частые заказы почти не лучше подстраиваются под фактический спрос и не окупают этих платежей.

I picked **candidate 2**. I estimated this in my head without simulating, so it rests on rough reasoning rather than exact numbers.

1. **Ordering every 3 days (candidates 0, 2, 3) beats the other schedules.**
   - **Daily orders (candidate 7):** 27 orders × 21 = 567 in order fees. That is about 378 more than ordering every 3 days, and it gives no real advantage, because the plan can't react to actual demand anyway.
   - **Every 2 days (candidate 5):** fees of 294, with nothing gained in return.
   - **Every 4 days (candidates 1, 4, 6):**
     - The warehouse fills exactly to 192 on product 1 arrival days, and in candidate 6 even 193. When demand is low, the surplus is simply lost on arrival.
     - A product 1 batch expires exactly when the next one arrives, so nothing carries over. Every miss turns into either spoilage at 7 per unit or a shortfall.
     - Total product 1 ordered is about 816 against expected demand of about 884.
   - **Every 3 days:** a product 1 batch sells for 3 days and still has a 4th day. Leftovers sell first on that day ("oldest stock first"), so overstocking costs little. Space is enough with room to spare.

2. **Comparing quantities with expected demand** (forecast × 1.046):
   - **Product 1, days 4–29, expected demand ≈ 884:**
     - candidate 0: 778, too little; at 5 per missing unit (lost margin plus penalty) that costs a lot;
     - candidate 2: 871, close to the target, given the trade-off of 5 per missing unit vs 7 per spoiled unit and the extra selling day;
     - candidate 3: 931, an excess that partly spoils.
   - **Product 0, days 3–29, expected demand ≈ 484:**
     - candidate 0: 463, with no safety margin, while a missing unit costs 11 (3 + 8);
     - candidate 2: 519, a reasonable buffer for a long-life product;
     - candidate 3: 579, about 95 units over. Most of that is left at the end and wasted (4 per unit plus 0.7 per day storage). The last batch of 69 alone covers demand of about 55 in days 27–29.

3. **Uncertainty:** candidate 2 has a moderate buffer for product 0, where shortfalls are expensive, and stays close to the target for product 1. It has no capacity risk. That makes it the most robust to ±30% swings in demand.

I picked **candidate 3**. I estimated this in my head, without running a simulation. Candidates 2 and 7 come out close to it, so the choice isn't certain.

- **Order cycle.** Orders every 4 days (candidates 1, 4, 6) keep more of item 0 in stock, and its holding cost is high (0.7). They also risk going over the 192-unit limit: item 0 arrives one day before item 1, so the two batches stack up on the shelves. Ordering every day (candidate 7) costs 21 × 27 = 567 in order fees alone. It also orders item 1 at only about 1.03 × the forecast, while average demand is 1.046 × the forecast, so it would often run short.
- **Order size within the 3-day cycle.** Running short of item 0 costs 11 per unit (8 penalty plus 3 lost margin). Leftovers carry over to the next cycle, so the cost of ordering too much is small. The best target comes out around 1.2 × the forecast for the 3-day window. Candidate 3 orders about 1.25× for item 0 and about 1.12× for item 1. Candidates 0 and 2 order closer to the forecast and would run short more often.
- **Risk.** Candidate 3 can occasionally go slightly over the 192-unit limit, around day 19. The loss from that is small.

I pick **candidate 5** (an order every 2 days). It's the most likely best, but not by a wide margin: by my rough estimate it beats daily ordering by only about 36 and the 3-day plans by about 130. I worked these out in my head, so random demand could change the order between 5, 7 and 2.

**Losses every plan shares.** Product 1 starts with 50 units, but days 0–3 need about 120, and the earliest new order lands on day 4. Product 0 starts with 22 against about 31 needed. So every plan pays penalties at the start, and this doesn't separate them.

**Ordering cost against holding cost:**
- Ordering on 27 days (candidate 7) costs 567 in fees, every 2 days (candidate 5) costs 294, and every 3 days (candidates 0, 2, 3) costs 189.
- Smaller, more frequent orders keep less stock on the shelf. Going from every 3 days to every 2 saves about 237 in holding for 105 more in fees, so candidate 5 comes out about 130 ahead of the 3-day plans.
- Daily ordering saves another ≈ 237 in holding against candidate 5 but costs 273 more in fees, so it's slightly worse.

**The every-4-days plans (1, 4, 6).** A product 1 order there has to cover exactly its 4-day shelf life, so anything left over expires. The batches are also close to the 192-unit warehouse limit, so units can be lost when an order arrives. They are the weakest group.

I estimate **Candidate 3** has the highest expected profit. I worked this out in my head without running anything, so these are approximate figures, not a full day-by-day simulation.

1. **How often to order.** Each day with an order costs 21.
   - Candidate 7 orders almost every day: 27 order days, about 567. Its quantities are fixed in advance, so ordering daily doesn't let it react to actual demand. It mostly just pays about 380 more than the every-3-days plans.
   - Candidate 5 orders every other day: 13 order days, about 273.
   - The every-3-days plans (0, 2, 3) have 9 order days, about 189. The every-4-days plans (1, 4, 6) have 7, about 147.

2. **Why every 4 days is worse.** Each 4-day batch of product 1 (expiry 4 days) has to cover exactly 4 days. Anything left over is thrown away, so every unsold unit costs its full price. A batch also arrives into an almost full warehouse: at Candidate 6's first product-1 arrival on day 4, stock reaches 192 of 192 on forecast demand. If demand runs a bit low, part of the delivery is lost on arrival. Those losses outweigh the 42 saved on two fewer order days.

3. **Why every 3 days works.** A product-1 batch covers 3 days, and whatever is left sells first on the 4th day, before it expires. Overstock is mostly not lost. The warehouse never gets close to full; the peak is about 167 units.

4. **Choosing among 0, 2 and 3.** Demand runs about 4.6% above forecast on average, and a product-0 shortage costs 8 per unit against a 3 margin. Product 0 keeps for 8 days, so a surplus mostly just carries over and costs 0.7 per unit per day in storage. Ordering generously is therefore worth it.
   - Candidate 3 orders about 1.2× forecast for product 0 and about 1.12× for product 1.
   - Candidate 2 orders about 1.1× and 1.03×.
   - Candidate 0 orders under forecast, about 0.92× for product 1, so it runs short most often.

   Candidate 3 is the most robust when demand comes in above forecast, and its downside when demand falls short is small.
